The Telepathy Tapes Silences Voices

The Telepathy Tapes: A Portal into a World of Woo

Stuart Vyse

From: Volume 50, No. 5
September/October 2026

Twitter Facebook
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 18:10
Instaread

The years 2024 and 2025 must have been a heady experience for documentary filmmaker Ky Dickens. In September 2024, she began releasing the ten-episode first season of her The Telepathy Tapes podcast. By December, the show started to appear on year-end lists of the best podcasts of 2024. Then lightning struck on Christmas Day. Based on hearing just two episodes, Joe Rogan (the undisputed king of podcasting, with millions of followers, who on this occasion happened to be wearing an elf costume) gave a brief favorable review of The Telepathy Tapes and expressed his belief that telepathy is real. Suddenly The Telepathy Tapes shot up the charts, briefly hitting number one and eclipsing the Joe Rogan Experience. By the end of January 2025, Dickens and the podcast had been signed with a talent agency (Katcy 2025).

In January 2025, Dickens released a series of “Talk Tracks” episodes that followed up with people from season one and introduced new paranormal ideas. Whereas season one had been released without advertising, Dickens’s new fame brought national sponsors and commercials for car insurance, mail order clothing, brassieres, CBD, microdose psilocybin (“magic mushrooms”) tea, and food delivery subscriptions. Later in 2025, The Telepathy Tapes website began offering a “backstage pass” subscription at $5.99 per month or $9.99 for “All Access” and various forms of merchandise, including hats, hoodies, and t-shirts. While on her summer tour, singer Ani DiFranco promoted the podcast and announced that she would be doing the music for the upcoming The Telepathy Tapes documentary film (KGNU Music 2025). Finally, as a tangible indication of its success, The Telepathy Tapes ended 2025 as the forty-first most popular podcast on Spotify, just below Pod Save America (forty) and three spots above Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend (forty-four) (Spangler 2025). Among 2025 Apple Podcasts, The Telepathy Tapes was the top podcast series, was the most shared podcast, and had the top podcast episode of the year: season one episode one.

All this is evidence that pseudoscience sells. As I have described in a previous article, season one of The Telepathy Tapes made the bold claim that nonspeaking individuals with profound autism are capable of communicating telepathically with their parents and teachers, as well as with each other (Vyse 2025a). Some could also communicate with the dead. As exciting as this sounds, there is one huge hitch: The purported telepathic messages were obtained using various forms of facilitated communication, the thoroughly debunked communication technique opposed by many professional and advocacy organizations, including the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (see facilitatedcommunication.org). For telepathic messages to be valid, the communication method used to report them must be valid. As a result, Dickens and the parents and teachers featured on the podcast exhibit two levels of unfounded belief: first in facilitated communication and second in telepathy.

An important secret of the success of The Telepathy Tapes is that it’s an audio podcast; listeners hear amazing descriptions of what is going on, but they can’t see the communication methods in use. Because Dickens’s original intent was to make a documentary film, all the material of season one was filmed, and for a ten-dollar fee, visitors to the podcast website are able to see a few video clips of what was happening. For analysis of some of those videos, see Janyce Boynton’s article “Debunking The Telepathy Tapes: The Role of Facilitator Behaviors” elsewhere in this issue.

Beyond Season One

Because most of the material of season one centered around a group of profoundly autistic children and adults, most of the paranormal phenomena presented was limited to them. But after season one, the guard rails fell off. Now it appears that any form of amazing woo is grist for The Telepathy Tapes mill. Along the way, we meet a long list of gurus, intuitives, and religious and spiritual guides. Inspirational writer and bestselling author of Eat Pray Love, Elizabeth Gilbert, makes an appearance (S2E21), but perhaps the best known of these thinkers is none other than Deepak Chopra, who is a classic purveyor of what psychologist Gordon Pennycook and colleagues call “pseudo-profound bullshit” (Pennycook et al. 2015). For example, in season one episode twenty-eight, Chopra insightfully declares that “consciousness does not exist in spacetime. Spacetime exists in consciousness. And if you start with that premise, that consciousness is the ontological primitive of the universe, then everything is easily explainable.”

Throughout the podcast, this kind of gauzy New Age talk is taken at face value, and anyone who has a scientific or skeptical approach is kept off stage and labeled a “materialist.” Ironically, this is the same epithet that was leveled at skeptics during the Spiritualist craze of the late nineteenth century. If your beliefs were based in nature and bounded by science, you were a materialist. In contrast, spiritualists believed that consciousness is not tied to the body and could both travel between bodies and persist after death. Interestingly, for people such as early psychologist and psychical researcher William James, telepathy was a bad thing because it represented an obstacle to proving the existence of an afterlife. If the medium at a séance were reporting information about a deceased target by reading the mind of the sitter rather than communicating with the dead, it would be an amazing skill, but it would not support the spiritualist hypothesis of life after death (Vyse 2025b). In the case of The Telepathy Tapes, the project is less about communication with the dead—although, there is some of that, too—and more about communication with parents and other people with autism who are still living; in that case, telepathy is just fine.

Magical Phenomena

Season two of The Telepathy Tapes credulously reports on many dazzling phenomena. Dickens introduced the new season by saying, “We’re opening up the next channel,” which seems to have been an understatement. Here are a few examples:

Telepathy with animals: A young competitive rider’s horse telepathically told her that he would not complete a particular jump because he was afraid it would hurt her. The rider was discovered to have juvenile arthritis, and when the arthritis was properly medicated, the horse was willing to do the jump (S2E5).

Telepathy with plants: A nonspeaking teen “says she’s been telepathically connected to plants since birth … offers herbal remedies no one taught her, identifies health issues her family hasn’t shared, and describes plant communication as naturally as breathing” (S2E6). Of course, these revelations were all obtained through a form of facilitated communication.

Remote viewing: Without ever having been to Korea, a New Jersey therapist was able to accurately describe a woman’s home in Korea, as well as where the woman was sitting at a particular moment. In addition, the therapist identified a corner of the house behind where the woman was sitting that was full of “very toxic energy” (S2E8).

Psychic surgery: A man described painlessly having a wisdom tooth removed by a Beijing dentist without anesthesia in less than a minute. Although no testimonials were provided in this case, the dentist also claimed to be able to extract teeth remotely (S2E8).

Energy healing: Actor Tim Daly (Wings, Madam Secretary) broke both his legs in a skiing accident, but he was up against a TV production schedule. He approached an energy healer who moved her hands over his legs, and he was able to go back to work “in about a week to ten days” (S2E8).

Telepathy with dementia patients: A man claimed people suffering from Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia sometimes contact him telepathically while he is driving his car. He was also able to communicate psychically with an Alzheimer’s patient with whom he did not share a common language (S2E10).

Mind sight: Children are said to be able to see things, read books, and identify objects while blindfolded. According to the podcast, even blind people can be taught to see with their minds (S2E11). Much of this mind-sight work is done with children, which raises ethical questions for me. What are the practical implications of teaching children (a) that they have magical powers or—assuming their powers aren’t magical—(b) to fool adults?

Near death experiences (NDEs) resulting in cancer cures (S2E12): There are many NDEs in The Telepathy Tapes, and most involve the typical features of bright white light, a feeling of warmth and love, and timelessness.

NDEs resulting in sudden savant artistic talents (S2E17 and S2E18): The importance given to sudden savant abilities in The Telepathy Tapes seems to be aimed at making an analogy to the sudden unexplained literacy of people who use facilitated communication. Given the great rarity of savants and the widely produced results of the spelling methods, the analogy seems quite weak to this listener.

The mechanism by which NDEs might cure cancer or produce sudden savantism is not explained, but these miracles both contribute to and draw upon the mystery surrounding NDEs.

When the podcast moved into health-related topics, the episodes began to include the necessary legal disclaimers, including “not FDA approved” and “don’t begin or stop any medical treatment without consulting your physician,” etc., but all manner of outlandish belief is given credulous coverage. Early in the podcast, Dickens describes herself as a skeptic, but after just a few episodes, she appeared to leave her skepticism behind. She often ends her episodes by saying “Please remember to stay kind, stay curious, and that being a true skeptic requires having an open mind.” She seems to have forgotten the full version of the motto adopted by many skeptics: “Keep an open mind, but not so open your brains fall out” (Farley 2014).

Throughout season two, these wild phenomena are bolstered by three philosophical frameworks. First, consistent with the rather vacuous statements by Deepak Chopra above, Dickens and others promote the view that consciousness is not attached to anything physical. Rather, it is the foundation of the universe. The physical world is a manifestation of our consciousness. To me this sounds like a rather egoistical and myopic assertion, but it is often repeated by various personalities on The Telepathy Tapes and proposed as a primary support for the reality of telepathy and communication with the dead. Second, Dickens and her guests frequently point to the untapped knowledge of ancient or indigenous peoples. Extracting teeth without anesthesia was accomplished with Qigong, which is part of traditional Chinese medicine; the herbal remedies of the nonspeaking girl are related to Native American medicine; and the remote viewing of the house in Korea was attributed to reiki, a form of Japanese energy healing that is also drawn from Qigong. Finally, there are several references to the newly discovered interstitium, a network of fluid-filled tubes throughout the body (Rettner and Livescience 2018). Dickens and guests argue—unpersuasively, in my view—that the discovery of this new organ somehow opens up new pathways of communication between individuals and new mechanisms for energy healing.

The Response to The Telepathy Tapes

Given the remarkable popularity of The Telepathy Tapes, it is likely that this podcast has done more than any other recent event to promote “spelling” (the term used to describe the latest variations of facilitated communication). This is nothing to sniff at. The parents and teachers who use these discredited methods mean well, but the profoundly handicapped children and adults subjected to them are being turned into marionettes to please the adults in their lives. The true humanity of these disabled individuals is being rejected in favor of a fantasy, and they are forced to endure many hours of manipulation rather than getting an appropriate education that would help them live as independently as possible.

Thankfully, this uplifting story of untapped intelligence and magical powers has not been greeted with uniform approval. An article on the British Psychological Society website in early November 2024, “Just Believe: The Strange Story of Facilitated Communication,” appears to have been the first strike against the podcast (Fisher 2024). Jonathan Jarry (2024) of the McGill University Office of Science and Society was next in line with an article in mid-December 2024, “The Telepathy Tapes Prove We All Want to Believe.” Additional critical articles appeared in the Guardian (Ryan 2025; Sawyer 2025), Vice (Busby 2025), and this magazine (Vyse 2025a). In addition, several podcasts and YouTube videos were quick to point to the podcast’s basis in a discredited form of communication.

Yes, there were also many adoring interviews with Dickens about The Telepathy Tapes, but the podcast’s great success also drew the attention of critics, which is a welcome development. Over the many years that facilitated communication and its variants have appeared in the news, the stories have almost always uncritically presented miraculous tales of discovered literacy and talent. The uplifting appeal of these stories—like the appeal of The Telepathy Tapes podcast itself—is just too attractive for news outlets to probe too deeply. I once met a documentary filmmaker who joked about “the fact too good to check.” That attitude appears to be a reality with so many of the writers of stories about facilitated communication. As a result, it is an encouraging sign that The Telepathy Tapes has received as much backlash as it has.

Status of the Documentary Film

Dickens’s background is in filmmaking, and from the beginning she said that the podcast was preliminary to the goal of making a documentary film about the users of these new forms of facilitated communication, people she calls “spellers” or “nonspeakers.” She has said she wants to do whatever she can to promote the use of these discredited methods, which she appears to accept as valid.

Dickens has periodically kept her listeners updated on the film’s progress, initially suggesting that it would be released in spring 2026; however, in an “ask me anything” segment of the podcast (S2E14), she indicated that various last-minute edits had pushed the completion date to summer 2026. According to posts on Dickens’s Instagram account, by February 2026, the film was very nearly completed. Ani DiFranco was indeed providing the music, and Dickens had held a few private screenings of an early cut of the film. As of this writing, there is no listing of the film on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb), and I have found no media mentions of distribution rights or theatrical release dates. It is possible Dickens intends to submit the film to festivals before settling on a distributor. In any case, people on both sides of this controversy will be anxious to see the completed documentary.

Conclusion

We live in dark times. In the United States, once-trusted government science agencies now spread anti-science, and conspiracy theories and paranormal beliefs long considered fringe are coming back. In this environment, The Telepathy Tapes may be more a symptom than a cause, but the success of the podcast is troubling. In addition to the forthcoming film, Dickens has said that there will be a season three of the podcast, and the show has already spun off a new YouTube program called “Now What?” which is aimed at parents of children with severe autism who are interested in the spelling techniques and want to explore the possibility that their children have telepathic abilities. It is also noteworthy that, in the second season of the podcast, Dickens began running commercials for an online homeschooling curriculum. Many parents who have sufficient resources have circumvented the rejection of facilitated communication by their local school systems by pulling their children out of school and teaching them at home. (See more on the homeschooling–facilitated communication connection in Katharine Beals’s article in this issue, “Telepathy via Facilitated Communication in Profound Autism: A 21st-Century Delusion.”)

If there is a bright spot to all this, it is that The Telepathy Tapes has not emerged unscathed. Many critics in the press and elsewhere are not falling for the world of woo presented in the podcast. To some degree, the success of The Telepathy Tapes has been its downfall, because its popularity has encouraged greater scrutiny, and I am confident that the release of the documentary film will be greeted with a new wave of reasoned critique. As Janyce Boynton’s article in this issue demonstrates, it is much harder to hide the flaws of facilitated communication on film than in an audio-only podcast. Whereas most previous presentations of facilitated communication in the press have been inspirational stories of miraculously discovered literacy, the response to The Telepathy Tapes has educated many people about the dangers of this pseudoscientific technique. Let’s hope that trend continues.

The Telepathy Tapes Silences Voices

Telepathy via Facilitated Communication in Profound Autism: A 21st-Century Delusion

Katharine Beals

From: Volume 50, No. 5
September/October 2026

Twitter Facebook

Belief in telepathy in autistic individuals, as promoted in The Telepathy Tapes podcast, stems from forces of modernity so inexorable that, were we to rewind the gears of history and try it all again, we’d end up right back where we are. The forces I’m implicating are disparate: the spread of literacy, the rise of the nuclear family, the disability rights and neurodiversity movements, trends in modern education, the accumulating research on autism, the “god-shaped hole” caused by growing secularism, the rise of mass media and then social media, the tendency of methodologies to evolve through implicit learning mechanisms and skeptical feedback toward increasing apparent plausibility, and, last but not least, the realities of profound autism.

But the most immediate reason widespread belief in autism telepathy was inevitable is that widespread belief in facilitated communication was inevitable.

The Inevitable Belief in Facilitated Communication

Facilitated communication (FC) is a pseudoscientific technique that purports to unlock language and literacy skills in nonspeaking or minimally speaking individuals with intellectual disabilities, particularly profound autism. A “facilitator” makes contact with the person’s body, moves around a letterboard, and/or hovers near the person and provides vocal and physical prompts and cues, while the person points to letters with an index finger. Through their touch, spoken prompts, gestures, and cues—however subtle and unintentional they may be—facilitators can completely control the messages their clients allegedly author.

But the extent of that control is not obvious to most people, and FC has long lurked as a theoretical solution to the enormous communication challenges of profound autism—challenges that have long resisted established therapies and teaching methods. FC’s adoption simply awaited motive and method. The spread of literacy skills and writing tools into most homes by the early twentieth century provided the method; the rise of nuclear families, together with the civil rights movement of the 1960s, provided the motive. One offshoot of civil rights was disability rights and the deinstitutionalization of children with cognitive disabilities, including profound autism (Braddock et al. 1990). Suddenly, large numbers of parents, especially mothers, were deeply invested as never before in the realities of profound autism. Not long afterward came the first public reports of facilitated pointing to letters by nonspeaking individuals (see Oppenheim 1974). Tellingly, the first messages that these “unlocked” individuals reportedly typed are just what parents long to hear: “I AM IN HERE”; “I AM INTELLIGENT”; “I LOVE YOU MOM AND DAD” (see “Prisoners of Silence” 1993).

But FC’s spread beyond isolated homes and clinics awaited its “professionalization,” that is, the emergence of FC practitioners and promoters with the resources and credentials to attract media attention. No sooner did these influencers emerge—Rosemary Crossley in Australia in the late 1970s and her protégé, Douglas Biklen, in the United States in the late 1980s—than the first FC crazes erupted (“Prisoners of Silence” 1993). But late twentieth-century FC, as yet untested by widespread scrutiny, looked crude and awkward: the facilitators mostly held their clients’ hands or wrists, and the clients often looked away while pointing. The fact that the public nonetheless took FC seriously speaks to the abiding thirst for stories of awakening—as well as to the intrigue of profound autism. The absent speech, or limited and often mysteriously echoic speech, along with the opaque body language, make profound autism a blank slate for wishful thinking. The most wishful thought of all—the notion of intact intelligence and language—dates back at least sixty years (Bettelheim 1967).

Still, some people raised questions about who was really authoring the messages. When the stakes were sufficiently high, some practitioners agreed to participate in facilitator-blinded message-passing tests. When these tests consistently showed facilitator authorship, FC version 1.0 was roundly discredited. But, in a testament to its resilience—indeed, its inevitability—FC never went away. It merely evolved.

FC evolved, in part, through the implicit learning that inevitably occurs during any kind of repeated practice. Longtime FC users learned to respond to ever more subtle cues, such that their facilitators could shift from hands and wrists to shoulders or backs—or in some instances merely hover close by and hold up the keyboard and/or move their own bodies around. FC evolved, in addition, through adjustments by promoters and practitioners in response to public scrutiny, the most salient manifestation of which was the rebranding of FC as rapid prompting method (RPM). RPM, which entered the Anglophone world in the early 2000s (Iversen 2006) and persists to this day, “corrected” many of the problematic optics, making FC look much more convincing, even in its initial stages with novice clients.

Most obviously, RPM has replaced hand or wrist holding with letterboard holding. Because observers tend to look at the person selecting letters rather than at the facilitator, the increased physical separation between the two parties makes the facilitator’s letter-cueing behaviors—board movements and gestures—much less salient. Second, RPM has replaced electronic keyboards with plastic letterboards, at least for the initial stages of FC. This has eliminated electronic transcriptions and allowed the facilitator, now doubling as a scribe who calls out and writes down letters, to decide when a letter was selected and which letter it was. Faulty judgments are hard for observers to notice unless they have a clear, head-on view of the letterboard and unless the facilitated person points slowly. Third, practitioners of RPM variants—the rebranding goes on, giving us spelling to communicate (S2C) and spellers method (“spelling”)—have had some success training facilitated individuals to look at letterboards when pointing (see Notaro 2023). Fourth, the 1990s debacle has deterred practitioners from participating in blind testing, and some FC certification programs require practitioners to sign agreements promising not to test the premises and claims (see Beals 2024).

All this has made FC 2.0 look much more convincing, especially to parents of profoundly autistic children, desperate as they still are for bigger improvements in communication than evidence-based methods have delivered (Brignell et al. 2018). But they aren’t alone. Facilitator cues are sometimes so subtle that even some autism experts have declared FC works for some autistic nonspeakers (Hemsley et al. 2025). And in the carefully filmed and edited videos that dominate YouTube, those cues can sometimes be practically invisible.

Meanwhile, a growing body of autism research now includes articles that have boosted FC’s scientific credibility. Earlier, FC proponents had to resort to mere assertions of their pro-FC claims, namely that rather than being the socio-cognitive disorder that its diagnostic criteria (informed by decades of clinical observation and empirical research) have defined it as, autism is instead some sort of motor disorder or body apraxia that impedes both speech and fine motor skills and is compounded by additional problems with sensory and emotional regulation (Biklen 1990). This purportedly accounts for the poor performance by those with profound autism on language tests; their inability to demonstrate comprehension by following directions; and their need for facilitators to help steady their arms, bypass their fine motor difficulties, and/or provide emotional, sensory, or attentional support through vocalizations and board movements (see the pro-FC website I-ASC.org). While no research supports any of this, some studies have found coordination difficulties and sensory sensitivities in autism, and proponents now routinely misconstrue these studies as validating FC (see Jaswal et al. 2020). Journalists and others ill-equipped to recognize misrepresentations of highly specialized research have readily accepted proponents’ sciencey-sounding claims that autism is a sensorimotor disorder or a type of apraxia.

Certain studies are especially popular with FC proponents. The fact that profound autism is randomly distributed across sectors of society means that it eventually gets diagnosed in the families of reputable researchers in psychology and neuroscience, some of whom have reacted by opting for FC—both personally and professionally. The resulting studies, biased and methodologically unsound though they are, have crept into academic journals and added to FC’s credibility (see Jaswal et al. 2020). Further securing that credibility is the staunch unwillingness of any of today’s practitioners to participate in blind testing.

The growing denial by the general public of the realities of intellectual disability is also FC-friendly. This mindset, part of a well-meaning, civil-rights-adjacent egalitarianism, has extended the idea that everyone is equally worthy to the idea that people are in some sense equally intelligent. The education world, in parallel, has extended the right of students with disabilities to an education, as stipulated by laws dating back to 1975, into a right to the same education that everyone else gets, as stipulated by the Every Student Succeeds Act of 2015. Teachers must now ensure that all but the most cognitively disabled 1 percent meet the same “challenging State academic standards” as specified by their state, and that the remaining 1 percent meet alternative standards that are still “aligned” with those “challenging state standards” (Every Student Succeeds Act 2015). Both expectations are problematic, but the second is especially so; it entails a deep denial by education policy makers of the realities of profound cognitive disabilities. Nowhere is that denial more evident than in Dynamic Learning Maps (DLM), a new computer-based assessment system currently in use in twenty states and intended as a Common Core alternative.

DLM’s chief purpose is to connect the dots between Common Core goals and alternative goals. It does so by extracting the so-called “essential elements” of the former and formulating three “precursor” goals (“initial,” “distal,” and “proximal”) that link more basic objectives to the essential elements. Consider the Common Core’s Fifth-grade Reading Literature goal (RL5.9), “Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (e.g., mysteries and adventure stories) on their approaches to similar themes and topics” (The Core Standards 2010). Per DLM as implemented by the State of Kansas, which has published this information online, the essential element is “Compare stories, myths, or texts with similar topics or themes.” Working backward, the proximal precursor is “Can identify and recall how characters’ actions affect the consequences that occur in the story afterwards”; the distal precursor is “Can understand adjectives in others’ speech”; and the initial precursor is “Can indicate an object when it is referred to by name” (Kansas Department of Education 2020). For fifth graders with the profound comprehension challenges inherent to profound autism, however, even the initial precursor can be totally elusive—even if applied only to the most basic of objects. By ninth grade, the initial precursors, items such as “Can identify the concrete details, such as individuals, events, or ideas in familiar informational texts,” are several orders of magnitude further out of reach.

Also combining unattainability with a reductio ad absurdum of general education content are DLM’s reading materials. Their topics are “drawn from texts that are often used in general education,” for example To Kill a Mockingbird. One of the texts drawn from To Kill a Mockingbird is Friends Are Great (ATLAS n.d.a). It consists of thirteen pages of sentences paired with photographs, and its first three sentences are exemplary (ATLAS n.d.b):

  • “Friends are great.”
  • “Friends help each other.”
  • “Friends can help each other study for school.”

While this text is orders of magnitude simpler than To Kill a Mockingbird, it is still beyond the comprehension skills of most profoundly autistic high school students, particularly the abstract, social word friend, which appears on every page.

To assess comprehension in Friends Are Great, the teacher first gathers objects that are related or unrelated to the story, reads the story, and points to the objects as their names come up. Then, page by page, the teacher rereads and asks questions, holding up pairs of objects as multiple-choice items. For the “Friends can help each other study for school” page, for example, the teacher holds up “one object that is used to study” and “another object that is unrelated to studying” and asks, “Which do you use to study?” (ATLAS n.d.b). DLM provides no guidelines on how to avoid unintentionally cueing the correct object, say by holding it closer to the student than the incorrect one—just as a facilitator might do with the target letter on a letterboard.

As for writing goals, DLM stipulates that all students need access to letter production, whether through pen and paper or through some sort of keyboard, even if they normally use non-alphabet–based augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) tools. As the video that details these options optimistically proclaims, “Everyone writes!” (ATLAS n.d.c).

Six years ago, I interviewed several dozen teachers of profoundly autistic students on various matters, and they uniformly decried the alternative goals and tests as a complete waste of time. Indeed, to anyone who knows anything about profound autism and takes a close look, the absurdities are patently obvious. But most people aren’t looking closely, and the assumption behind these policies—the denial of intellectual disability—extends far beyond education world groupthink.

Other manifestations of that denial are the pseudoscientific notions of multiple intelligences and learning styles, which have recast cognitive strengths and weaknesses as differences in cognitive style (see Newton and Miah 2020). These have readily caught on with the general public, as has the neurodiversity movement’s recasting of autism, including profound autism, as neurological differences rather than deficits (Kapp et al. 2013). Now many teachers and others consider all students to be equally capable but uniquely different, with different students simply needing different ways to “demonstrate understanding”: an essay for the “verbal”; a diorama for the “visual”; and a dance for the “bodily-kinesthetic” (Boutelier and Smalligan 2018). From here, it is a short step to objects or letterboards for “neurodiverse” learners to point to.

As of this writing, letterboards are a bridge too far; parents have had only limited success getting schools to accept them. But two other trends have helped boost FC use with school-aged children: the loosening regulations around homeschooling and the rise of online schools and classes (Molnar et al. 2023; Texas Homeschool Coalition 2025). Only some online schools accept FC, but no one is routinely monitoring private homes to validate the authorship of online submissions or homeschool portfolios.

The extension of “different but equal” to profound autism has been vital in boosting FC. So has another popular notion that harks back to the century-old progressive education movement that began as a reaction against traditional, teacher-centered “drill and kill” classrooms and continues to this day. This is the largely pseudoscientific notion that students can acquire academic skills without direct instruction and become literate through print-rich environments (see Christodoulou 2013). Together, these address the one glaring question that persists even in the most convincing instances of FC 2.0: How have facilitated nonspeakers acquired the sophisticated vocabulary and informational content that appears in so many of their FC-generated messages? How can people who haven’t had any formal instruction in spelling, vocabulary, or natural history spell, understand, and intend to communicate words such as poignant and amber? The purported answer is that they, like everyone else, can learn by osmosis.

The more credible FC 2.0 becomes, the more it inspires credulous accounts, and the more people start using it. Conversely, the more credulous accounts there are, the more credible it becomes, and the more people start using it. With the rise of platforms such as YouTube, the emergence of influencers with personal ties to profound autism and FC 2.0, and a public always hungry for feel-good news, we now have a steady stream of stories about letterboards unlocking communication and social connection—the two things that every parent wants most.

And so it is that many people, inevitably, believe in FC—so much so that the most iconic images of profound autism in post-industrial society are no longer of children in institutions wearing white linens or straightjackets but of children out in the real world spelling out poetry and pro-FC advocacy on held-up letterboards.

Why Widespread Belief in Autism Telepathy Is Inevitable

Reports of autism telepathy are nearly as old as FC (see Janyce Boynton’s article in this issue). The largely subconscious control by facilitators over messages means that some facilitators will inevitably start noticing their own thoughts, spelling quirks, and/or private knowledge occasionally leaking out onto letterboards. The reason for this leakage, of course, is too hard to face, particularly if the facilitator (as is so often the case) is also the parent. So a red flag for facilitator control becomes a revelation of something far more uplifting: My child can read my thoughts.

What has changed since these first reports is the huge increase in FC use; this has drastically increased the numbers of facilitators who think their children or clients are telepathic. FC groups on social media provide a venue for disclosing impressions and finding others who share them. Gaining confidence in numbers and reassurances that their revelations aren’t crazy, some start disclosing them to outsiders. Eventually, those revelations reach a rogue neurologist who starts doing telepathy experiments. Those experiments catch the attention of an established producer who deems it fruitful to make a podcast about telepathy in individuals with profound autism (Jarry 2024). The only question is why such a podcast would win over so many people with no personal stake in profound autism or autism telepathy—especially if it provides minimal video documentation to support its extraordinary oral testimonials about telepathic communication.

Consider, first, the so-called “god-shaped hole” left in many people’s minds by a world that has increasingly abandoned traditional religion: a vacuum into which a variety of pseudoscientific convictions have already rushed (Partridge 2006). Where there are beliefs about energy healing and alien visitations, there is plenty of room for telepathy. Remember, next, the tabula rasa of profound autism. This permits fantasies not just that autistic nonspeakers are intellectually and linguistically intact but that they’re also spiritually gifted. Consider, finally, what may be the most convincing factor: the voices of the parents. They sound sincere, sympathetic, and totally convinced (presumably because they are convinced) that the telepathy they are witnessing is real.

All the messages that purportedly show telepathic ability in The Telepathy Tapes podcast and its videos, of course, are generated through FC 2.0 (Vyse 2025). This telepathy-mediating FC has been refined by years of conditioning of facilitated people to respond to increasingly subtle cues and years of adjustments by proponents in response to public scrutiny. Carefully chosen camera angles and carefully timed cuts make it difficult (if not impossible) for most viewers to spot the letter-directing cues. If, as some have claimed, there is simply no way for the messages to be controlled by cues that they themselves can’t detect, then there is no other explanation. All the profoundly autistic nonspeakers on the podcast—and probably many others as well—must be telepathic.

But even for those denizens of twenty-first-century post-industrial society who haven’t (yet) fallen hard for telepathy, it is hard to accept that something far more sinister is afoot.
